compareMetricEpsDilutedDefinition: Profit divided by the number of shares.
compareMetricEpsDilutedWhyMatters: Shows how profit per share changes over time and feeds the P/E ratio. It is not comparable between two companies, because each has a different number of shares.
compareMetricFreeCashFlowDefinition: Cash the business brought in after paying for new equipment and buildings.
compareMetricFreeCashFlowWhyMatters: The cash that can pay dividends, buy back shares or pay down debt.
compareMetricGrossMarginDefinition: How much of each sales dollar is left after paying for the product itself.
compareMetricGrossMarginWhyMatters: A high number usually means people pay up for what the company sells.
compareMetricNetIncomeDefinition: The profit left after every cost, interest and tax.
compareMetricNetIncomeWhyMatters: The money that belongs to shareholders.
compareMetricNetMarginDefinition: How much of each sales dollar ends up as profit after every cost, interest and tax.
compareMetricNetMarginWhyMatters: The bottom line. It is the profit that can pay dividends or buy back shares.
compareMetricOperatingMarginDefinition: How much of each sales dollar is left after running the business: product, staff, research and marketing.
compareMetricOperatingMarginWhyMatters: Shows how efficiently the company is run day to day.
compareMetricRevenueDefinition: Everything customers paid the company over the period, before any costs.
compareMetricRevenueGrowthDefinition: How much sales grew in the latest fiscal year compared with the year before.
compareMetricRevenueGrowthWhyMatters: Growing sales usually means more customers or higher prices.
compareMetricRevenueWhyMatters: The simplest measure of how big the business is.
compareMetricShareholdersEquityDefinitio: What the company owns minus what it owes.
compareMetricShareholdersEquityWhyMatter: Companies that buy back a lot of their own shares can have low equity while doing well.
compareMetricTotalAssetsDefinition: Everything the company owns: cash, buildings, equipment, investments and more.
compareMetricTotalAssetsWhyMatters: More is not better on its own. Some great businesses need very little.

economicWhy_jobs: How many jobs the US added last month, plus the unemployment rate. A surprise either way changes what the market expects the Fed to do with interest rates.
economicWhy_cpi: How fast prices are rising for consumers. Inflation above expectations raises the odds of higher interest rates, which tends to hit growth stocks hardest.
economicWhy_ppi: How fast prices are rising for businesses. It often hints at where consumer inflation is heading next.
economicWhy_jolts: How many jobs employers are trying to fill. Fewer openings can be an early sign that the job market is cooling.
economicWhy_claims: How many people filed for unemployment benefits last week. It is the most up to date read on layoffs.
economicWhy_fomc: The Federal Reserve announces its interest rate decision, followed by a press conference. Rates set borrowing costs and change how investors value every stock.
economicWhy_gdp: The broadest measure of how fast the US economy is growing. A big surprise in either direction can move the whole market.
economicWhy_pce: The inflation measure the Fed watches most closely, released with data on income and spending. It weighs heavily on where rates go next.

economicLessonBigFour: The Big Four: Rates, Jobs, Inflation, Oil
economicLessonRates: Why Rate Hikes Hit Growth Stocks Harder
economicExplainWhat_jobs: The Employment Situation report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It counts how many jobs US employers added last month, and gives the unemployment rate and how fast wages are growing.
economicExplainWhy_jobs: Jobs drive spending, and spending drives company profits. The Fed watches it closely too, because a job market that is running hot can keep inflation high.
economicExplainWatch_jobs: What moves markets is the gap between the real number and what economists expected. Good news can be bad news: very strong hiring can push stocks down if investors think it keeps interest rates high for longer.
economicExplainWhat_cpi: The Consumer Price Index tracks how the prices of everyday things, like food, rent and gas, changed over the past month and year. That change is inflation.
economicExplainWhy_cpi: Inflation decides what the Fed does with interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and make future profits worth less today, which weighs on stock prices.
economicExplainWatch_cpi: Look at core CPI, which leaves out food and energy because their prices jump around. A hotter reading than expected usually pushes stocks down, fast-growing tech companies most of all.
economicExplainWhat_ppi: The Producer Price Index tracks the prices businesses get for their goods and services, before those costs reach shoppers.
economicExplainWhy_ppi: When costs rise for businesses, they often pass them on to customers later. That makes PPI an early hint of where consumer inflation is heading.
economicExplainWatch_ppi: It usually moves markets less than CPI. It matters most when it surprises in the same direction as other recent inflation numbers.
economicExplainWhat_jolts: The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey counts open jobs, hires and people quitting. It covers the month before last, so it runs a little behind the jobs report.
economicExplainWhy_jolts: Lots of openings means employers are competing for workers, which pushes wages and inflation up. Falling openings can be an early sign that the economy is slowing.
economicExplainWatch_jolts: The number of openings and how many people quit. People quit more when they are confident they can find a better job, so a falling quit rate points to a cooling job market.
economicExplainWhat_claims: Every Thursday the Department of Labor reports how many people filed for unemployment benefits for the first time in the week before.
economicExplainWhy_claims: It is the most up to date signal on layoffs. A steady rise can show the job market weakening before the monthly jobs report does.
economicExplainWatch_claims: A single week can be noisy, especially around holidays. Investors watch the trend over several weeks rather than one number.
economicExplainWhat_fomc: The Federal Open Market Committee is the group at the Federal Reserve that sets US interest rates. It announces its decision at 2:00 PM ET, and the Fed chair takes questions at a press conference half an hour later.
economicExplainWhy_fomc: The Fed rate is the starting point for what it costs to borrow almost everywhere, from mortgages to company loans. A change ripples through stocks, bonds and currencies.
economicExplainWatch_fomc: The decision itself is usually expected ahead of time. What moves prices is often the wording of the statement and what the chair hints about the next few meetings. Four meetings a year also publish the Fed's own forecasts for rates and the economy.
economicExplainWhat_gdp: Gross domestic product is the total value of everything the US economy produced in a quarter. The first estimate comes about a month after the quarter ends and is revised twice after that.
economicExplainWhy_gdp: It is the broadest scorecard for the economy. Growing GDP usually means growing company sales, while two shrinking quarters in a row is a common sign of a recession.
economicExplainWatch_gdp: The first estimate, called the advance estimate, gets the most attention. The later revisions tend to move markets less.
economicExplainWhat_pce: The Personal Income and Outlays report shows how much Americans earned and spent last month. It includes the PCE price index, another measure of inflation.
economicExplainWhy_pce: PCE is the inflation measure the Fed uses for its 2% target, so it carries a lot of weight in interest rate decisions.
economicExplainWatch_pce: Watch core PCE, which leaves out food and energy. CPI usually comes out first, so PCE moves markets most when it tells a different story.

compareMetricHealthScoreDefinition: BullPen’s 0 to 100 score for how sound a business looks, built from profit, debt, growth, cash flow, price and risk.
compareMetricHealthScoreWhyMatters: A quick first check. Open the stock page to see which parts pull the score up or down.
compareMetricMarketCapDefinition: What the whole company is worth on the stock market today: the share price times the number of shares.
compareMetricMarketCapWhyMatters: Bigger is not better. It tells you how much the market thinks the company is worth, not how good an investment it is.
compareMetricPeRatioDefinition: The share price divided by one year of profit per share. A P/E of 25 means you pay $25 for every $1 the company earns in a year.
compareMetricPeRatioWhyMatters: Lower means you pay less for each dollar of profit. A high P/E often means investors expect fast growth.
compareMetricDividendYieldDefinition: The cash a company pays its shareholders each year, as a share of the stock price. 2% means $2 a year for every $100 you own.
compareMetricDividendYieldWhyMatters: Income you get without selling. Many fast-growing companies pay none and reinvest instead.
